article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : London-based SC Films International has struck a slew of international deals on animated family-adventure Cloud Girl (previously known as Girl in the Clouds ).

The feature from French writer-director Philippe Riche was inspired by Romain Puértolas’ 2015 novel The Little Girl Who Swallowed a Cloud as Big as the Eiffel Tower and screened as an Official Selection of the 2026 Annecy International Animation Film Festival.

Viva Pictures will release the film in U.S. cinemas on January 8, 2027. Pan Distribution has taken rights for France, Pathé Films for French-Speaking Switzerland and O’Brother for Benelux.

Related Stories

Lilly Wachowski Boards Comedy 'Making A Bridesmaid' As Project Heads To AFM For Sales

Celine Dion To Perform Paul McCartney's Original Songs For Animated Feature 'High In The Clouds'

The latest international buyers include Baltics (Acme), Bulgaria (Pro Films), CIS (Volga), Czech Republic & Slovakia (Bohemia Motion Pictures), Former Yugoslavia (Blitz), Greece (The Film Group), Israel (FilmHouse), Latin America and South Africa (Sun Distribution Group), Middle East (ECS), Poland (Kinoswiat), Portugal (Cinemundo), Romania (Cay Films), Hungary (ADS), Scandinavia (Mislabel), Turkey (Film Medya), Ukraine (Adastra), North Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa (Pathé Touch Afrique). Sales will continue at the American Film Market next month.

Watch on Deadline

Cloud Girl tells the story of an 11-year-old avid reader entrusted with a magical quill that can grant any wish it writes. When she wishes to fly and for her guinea pig, Airbag, to talk, the duo embarks on a dangerous adventure to save the planet.

The English-speaking voice cast is led by Faith Delaney ( Hamnet ), Hugh Laurie ( House ), Joseph Balderrama ( F1: The Movie ) Ken Nwosu ( Greenland 2: Migration ) and Bhavnisha Parmar ( Doctor Who ).

Pic is produced by Brio Films, Panama Productions, Scope Pictures, and Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes Cinéma, with the support of Canal +, Eurimages, and CNC. Stim Studio is the lead animation studio. Luc Bossi is producer; executive producers are Simon Crowe, Jon Goldman and Valérie Leroux; co-producers are Lhoussaïne Zammat, Geneviève Lemal, Félix Ferrand, Julien Seul, Sawsan Asfari, Audrey Abiven, Luc Hardy, Nicolas Corouge, Pascal Laik and Elisabeth Bykoff.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s an exciting time for Japanese cinema, with franchise hits from Demon Slayer to Godzilla stomping around the world, and Japanese arthouse titles taking the spotlight at major film festivals including Venice, Toronto and Cannes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This year’s Tokyo Film Festival , taking place in the Hibiya-Ginza district of the city from October 26 to November 4, aims to take full advantage of the momentum and help expand the international profile of Japanese films. While Ichiyama has been strengthening the festival’s competitions, Gala and World Focus line-ups, Hisamatsu says he wants to bolster the glamour quotient at the festival, especially as it gears up for its 40th edition next year."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Watch on Deadline"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We want to combine art and entertainment and make the festival as multifaceted as possible,” says Hisamatsu, sitting down with Deadline at the festival’s office in the historic Togeki Building in Ginza. “This should be a festival for cinephiles, for general film fans, and also for people who maybe only visit a cinema once or twice in a year. Everyone should be able to find something they want to see.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While describing this year’s pre-anniversary edition as a time for evaluation, he envisages a line-up that includes Japanese films, Hollywood and other international titles, awards contenders, and every genre and format from live action and animation to documentary and short films. The U.S. studios have not been promoting heavily at Asian film festivals in recent years, but Hisamatsu hopes to lure them back: “Japan is still a big market – last year our box office hit a record and surpassed pre-pandemic revenues. Now is a good time to reboot the popularity of Hollywood films in Japan.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hisamatsu is also engaging with international organisations, including the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences ( AMPAS ), which is bringing a delegation of executives, including Academy CEO Bill Kramer, to participate in a busy schedule of panels and networking events at the festival. Several awards season contenders, including Wild Horse Nine , La Bola Negra , animated feature Wildwood , and Christian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord , are screening across the festival’s Gala, World Focus and Special Screenings sections.", "links": [{"text": "AMPAS", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/ampas/"}, {"text": "busy schedule of panels and networking events", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/oscars-ampas-bill-kramer-toho-hiro-matsuoka-1237156496/"}, {"text": "Wild Horse Nine", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/wild-horse-nine/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Wild-Horse-Nine-OMNI.jpg?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "‘Wild Horse Nine’ Searchlight Pictures", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "However, the festival toppers stress that this doesn’t mean any attention will be taken away from Japanese titles. “One of our major goals is to introduce Japanese films to international markets,” says Hisamatsu. Korean filmmaker Yang Sang-ho’s zombie thriller Colony will close the festival.", "links": [{"text": "Godzilla Minus Zero", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/godzilla-minus-zero/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Three Japanese films have been selected for the festival’s main Competition section: The Canary’s Lullaby , directed by Akira Ikeda; Yukiko Mishima’s Two Cigarettes, Three Nights ; and Akira Yamamoto’s The Intertwining . Singaporean animation Magic Atlas from Sun Xun, and Trees Are Watching from Iranian-Kurdish filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Heysel-85.jpg?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "‘Heysel 85’", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer is heading the main competition jury, which also includes Tokyo and New York-based producer Alex Lo, Korean producer Oh Jungwan, French colorist Yov Moor and Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe. article_text:
It’s an exciting time for Japanese cinema, with franchise hits from Demon Slayer to Godzilla stomping around the world, and Japanese arthouse titles taking the spotlight at major film festivals including Venice, Toronto and Cannes.

This year’s Tokyo Film Festival , taking place in the Hibiya-Ginza district of the city from October 26 to November 4, aims to take full advantage of the momentum and help expand the international profile of Japanese films. Under incoming Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu, and Programming Director Shozo Ichiyama, the festival is also positioning itself as a launchpad for international films in Japan.

Related Stories

Amazon MGM Studios Japan To Double Investment In Original Content; ‘One Piece’ & ‘Kingdom’ Producers Talk IP Strategies – TIFFCOM

Yuriko Gamo Romer & Marc Smolowitz On The 12 Year Journey Behind Their Japanese-U.S. History Baseball Doc ‘Diamond Diplomacy’ — Tokyo

Hisamatsu, who previously held senior posts at Warner Bros Japan and local studio Shochiku, headed the festival from 2017-2021 and returned earlier this year when Hiroyasu Ando stepped down after seven years at the helm. While Ichiyama has been strengthening the festival’s competitions, Gala and World Focus line-ups, Hisamatsu says he wants to bolster the glamour quotient at the festival, especially as it gears up for its 40th edition next year.

Watch on Deadline

“We want to combine art and entertainment and make the festival as multifaceted as possible,” says Hisamatsu, sitting down with Deadline at the festival’s office in the historic Togeki Building in Ginza. “This should be a festival for cinephiles, for general film fans, and also for people who maybe only visit a cinema once or twice in a year. Everyone should be able to find something they want to see.”

While describing this year’s pre-anniversary edition as a time for evaluation, he envisages a line-up that includes Japanese films, Hollywood and other international titles, awards contenders, and every genre and format from live action and animation to documentary and short films. The U.S. studios have not been promoting heavily at Asian film festivals in recent years, but Hisamatsu hopes to lure them back: “Japan is still a big market – last year our box office hit a record and surpassed pre-pandemic revenues. Now is a good time to reboot the popularity of Hollywood films in Japan.”

Hisamatsu is also engaging with international organisations, including the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences ( AMPAS ), which is bringing a delegation of executives, including Academy CEO Bill Kramer, to participate in a busy schedule of panels and networking events at the festival. Several awards season contenders, including Wild Horse Nine , La Bola Negra , animated feature Wildwood , and Christian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord , are screening across the festival’s Gala, World Focus and Special Screenings sections.

However, the festival toppers stress that this doesn’t mean any attention will be taken away from Japanese titles. “One of our major goals is to introduce Japanese films to international markets,” says Hisamatsu. The festival will open with a Japanese film – Zeze Takahisa’s Sukiyaki , about the historic song that topped the Billboard charts and remains one of the world’s best-selling tunes – while Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus Zero , the highly-anticipated sequel to Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One , will play as the Centerpiece Film. Korean filmmaker Yang Sang-ho’s zombie thriller Colony will close the festival.

Three Japanese films have been selected for the festival’s main Competition section: The Canary’s Lullaby , directed by Akira Ikeda; Yukiko Mishima’s Two Cigarettes, Three Nights ; and Akira Yamamoto’s The Intertwining . Ichiyama, the festival’s Programming Director, explains that The Canary’s Lullaby is a Japan-Taiwan co-production, partly filmed on Taiwan’s Kinmen Island, and The Intertwining is based on a Japanese novel but has Korean elements, demonstrating the more international outlook of Japan’s new generation of directors.

With major festivals including Cannes, Venice and Toronto, all of which take place before Tokyo, hoovering up Japanese titles over the past few years, Ichiyama says his focus has been on discoveries, as the festival requires world premieres for the Japanese films in competition. “These three filmmakers are not so well known internationally, but they’re all extremely promising, and have the potential to go to European film festivals in the future,” he says.

Other world premieres in the Competition line-up include Indonesian filmmaker Garin Nugroho’s Red Before Dawn , set in a newly independent Indonesia in the 1940s, which Ichiyama describes as “a big-budget epic drama”; Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski’s social satire Sister Brother Manhole Cover ; and two Chinese-language titles Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting , from Qiu Jiongjiong, and Wang Jianyong’s The Night That Binds Us .

Also in the line-up of 15 competition titles is Rubaiyat Hussain’s The Difficult Bride , which world premiered in the Horizons section of this year’s Venice film festival and marks the first ever Bangladeshi film selected for Tokyo main competition. “We saw it in Venice and sent the the invitation very quickly,” says Ichiyama. “We usually see two or three interesting films from Bangladesh in one year, and this one is outstanding.”

Rounding out the competition are Heysel 85 , from Romanian filmmaker Teodora Ana Mihai, joining Tokyo Competition for the third time following Traffic and La Civil ; Until The Day Ends , from Serbian filmmaker Jelena Maksimović; Double Freedom , from Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso; Even If Hell Came , from Italy’s Samuele Rossi; Portuguese filmmaker Sérgio Graciano’s Memories Of Prison ; Singaporean animation Magic Atlas from Sun Xun, and Trees Are Watching from Iranian-Kurdish filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi.

Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer is heading the main competition jury, which also includes Tokyo and New York-based producer Alex Lo, Korean producer Oh Jungwan, French colorist Yov Moor and Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe. An Australia Spotlight will screen De Heer’s 2022 The Survival Of Kindness ; Natalie Erika James’ body horror Saccharine , and Vee Shi’s hybrid documentary Time And Tide .

Other talent attending the festival include Cate Blanchett , in town to celebrate the Japan premieres of five short films supported by the Displacement Film Fund (and who is also a producer on Alpha Gang , recently added to Special Screenings); as well as Iranian director Mohammad Rasoulof and Japanese filmmaker Mipo O, both recipients of this year’s Kurosawa Akira Award. Filmmakers including Ilya Khrzhanovsky ( DAU ), Teodora Ana Mihai ( Heysel 85 ), Zeze Takahisa ( Sukiyaki ), Shahrbanoo Sadat ( No Good Men ) and Yukiko Sode ( All The Lovers In The Night ) will deliver talk sessions and masterclasses.

Tokyo has two other competition sections – Asian Future, focused on emerging Asian directors, and Nippon Cinema Now, which aims to present an overview of the current state of contemporary Japanese film. Nippon Cinema Now will screen eight titles, from both new and established directors, and has introduced two new awards for Best Film and a Special Jury Prize.

Asian Future, programmed by Kenji Ishizaka, will screen 10 world premieres from Japan, Korea, Philippines, India, Turkey, Kazakhstan, Indonesia and Iran. This year also sees the return of the festival’s non-competitive section dedicated to Southeast Asian cinema, Crosscut Asia, held in partnership with the Japan Foundation, which stopped running during the pandemic period. Now titled Crosscut Asia+, the section will screen three recent festival hits, Four Seasons In Java , Filipiñana and Becoming Human , along with a selection of retrospective titles.

Other major sections include Animation, which will screen Cannes Un Certain Regard special jury prize winner Iron Boy , among other titles; Women’s Empowerment, including recent festival breakouts Lovers In The Blue Night , from India’s Anupama Roy, and A Girl Unknown , from China’s Zou Jing; Japanese Classics, including a Kenji Mizoguchi retrospective; and the Youth and Asian Students Film Conference sections.

Taking place towards the end of the year, Tokyo Film Festival has always been in a good position to present a “best of fests” round-up for local audiences, and this year aims to double down on efforts to connect international films with Japanese buyers, both directly at the festival and through the TIFFCOM contents market taking place a few metro stops away.

“Especially in World Focus, we’re showing many films that played in Berlin, Venice and Cannes, several of which have still not found a Japanese distributor,” Ichiyama says. “Japan has many strong, independent buyers, but with the current weakness of the Japanese yen, they’ve not been so eager to travel to Venice and Toronto or acquire new films. We can present those titles here in theatres with local audiences and Japanese subtitles.”

With many screenings already sold out, filmmakers and industry can expect packed houses and attentive audiences for these films. As Hisamatsu observes, Japan continues to be one of the world’s top theatrical markets, and while anime and Godzilla may be pulling the biggest crowds, Tokyo Film Festival is one time of year at least when movies of all genres, languages and budget levels will be reaching audiences on a big screen.

The festival kicks off on Monday, October 26, with an opening ceremony and screening of Sukiyaki, and runs until Wednesday, November 4, while TIFFCOM is taking place October 28-30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho.

editorial_title_zh: “永远不够大”：走近蓬勃发展的阴茎增大产业
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在一部极具启发性的纪录片中，一个受“外貌至上”（looksmaxxing）影响、将“你的社会资本与外表挂钩”的世界，促使越来越多的男性渴望更多。人类对自身尺寸的痴迷古已有之，高耸的建筑、或奉承（大雕能量）或冒犯（混蛋）的影射，以及历代无数崇拜男性雄风的器物——比如某位色情明星对唐纳德·特朗普“毒蕈”阴茎的描述——都将其彰显无遗。

article_text:
M an’s obsession with his member is a tale as old as time, writ large in sky-scraping edifices, in allusions that flatter (big dick energy) or offend (prick), in the countless artifacts across the ages that venerate male potency – a porn star’s description of Donald Trump’s “toadstool” penis. But it’s the booming intimate wellness industry – AKA the rash (ahem) of fillers, therapies and cosmetic procedures that have come into vogue since the little blue pill rocked the market – that most intrigued Daniel Lombroso, the esteemed documentarian who made his name at the Atlantic and the New Yorker dissecting male fragility.

“A lot of the stories I worked on at those places were kind of fringy subculture and oftentimes adjacent to white nationalism,” says Lombroso, who became aware of the rising demand for penile enhancement procedures while reporting on plastic surgery trends at the New Yorker. “I started calling all these practitioners. But to make an embedded film the way I do, you need someone who’s very open.”

A 2024 study of US Google searches noted an increase in interest in penile-enhancement injections from 2013 through 2022. Lombroso’s 90-minute film, Manhood, puts male self-esteem issues at the heart of the trend on a cold, chafing examination table. Our guide throughout is Bill Moore, a capitalist in scrubs who gives fresh meaning to the phrase bedside manner. We meet him at home, tongue-kissing a pet lap dog while snuggled up under the covers with his male partner. We behold the full splendor of his naked body, nipped and tucked in retreat from the ravages of time and his own unforgiving eye. “Nobody would suspect I’ve ever had anything done!” he says with bracing cluelessness.

We see Moore hawk outpatient penile enhancement procedures from his Dallas strip mall office for $15,000 and $20,000 a pop and tout the lowly glow-ups as career-changing, sex-life turbocharging, depression-curing – whatever patients need to hear to fork over the dough, really. “Everybody wants a boat that’s one foot longer,” one guy says as Moore sticks a long numbing needle into his nether regions. “The boat is never big enough.”

We see many of these patients (though customers is the better word, since, again, Moore is not a doctor), their faces more obscured than their ink-marked private parts. The inclination toward anonymity owes as much to the physical embarrassment Moore’s clientele bring into the room as to the irony of receiving this kind of care from an out-and-proud gay man – the megachurch pastor, the border patrol agent. It’s wild to see Moore act as a machismo whisperer to men who might perceive him as less than masculine, especially as he reflects on the guilt and fear of rejection he experienced before coming out to conservative Christian family members in the deep south (not that his mother having dementia doesn’t help).

Throughout the film, Lombroso manages to point out these and other paradoxes without casting judgment. “I’m not deep in the looksmaxxing world, but part of what Clavicular and those guys understand is that your social capital is tied to your appearance,” Lombroso says. “Does your penis size matter? Probably not. But there are all these stats about the huge percentage of American men who obsess over it, which was foreign to me. And it connects all these other things we talk about – like how many older American men don’t know how to make a best friend.”

None of Moore’s customers embodies male loneliness quite like Ruben, a father of five who is so desperate to enlarge his penis that he moves his family in with an ex to raise money for an enhancement procedure. “I have to sell my house this weekend, and I’m going to Bill after.” Lombroso recalls Ruben telling him in a phone call. “I was like, ‘OK, I’ll be there tomorrow.’ The only way to make a film like this, because I’m in New York and this was in Texas, was to fly out on a whim every time and just capture things as they happened.”

Ruben fills his days listening to Joe Rogan prattle on about the marginalization of manly men and spends nights performing at comedy open mics in bars to crickets – and zero friends in the crowd. His jokes about child abuse are as wince-inducing as the circular logic of upgrading his manhood. He believes it will help protect and provide for his family, even as it fundamentally destabilizes them. “He’s actually a very loving father,” Lombroso says. “A good guy. But he escapes into these worlds like many of us do, and I think eventually it caught up to him.”

Meanwhile, Lana, Ruben’s poor wife, overwhelmed by the succession of shocks his big dick sidequest has imposed on their lives, is pushed ever closer to divorce. “With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this,” Lombroso says. “You see Lana kind of against it, but not taking too strong of a stance.”

But the film takes its strangest turn with David, a handsome young man who seeks out Moore’s help repairing the damage from an enhancement procedure botched by another dubious quasi-physician – Victor Loria, a gruff George Costanza-type who brags about growing up in a “connected” family (“We lived the Goodfellas life,” he says, wondering “when are we going to jail, basically”) and keeps a large malpractice insurance disclaimer nailed to his front office wall like Martin Luther’s 95 Theses. Loria is the film’s villain, in case that wasn’t clear.

David seems plucked from a casting call for the reality TV series Botched, a naive keen to hit control-Z after going under the knife too young and, perhaps, steer others away from rushing down that same path. But as his arc unfolds and his OnlyFans porn-acting past is revealed, it turns out he and Moore have more in common than just deeply religious parents who viewed homosexuality as an abomination. They share a bed, too – with Moore’s partner and the dog. That David risks permanent damage from this corrective procedure only heightens the stakes around the throuple bombshell.

Lombroso calls the effort to compel David’s participation in the film “one of the hardest acts of persuasion I’ve ever done. It took the entire film to convince him. We were going to use AI face replacement. But right around the rough-cut stage, when we realized he was the heartbeat of the story, we flew him into New York and showed him – and he loved it. Told his family everything. Now he’s touring with the film. It’s the best.”

Weaving between David’s feelgood story, Loria’s villainy and Ruben’s allegory is Moore – the honest broker who still lulls customers into thinking he’s a doctor, who travels to conferences to show actual doctors how to get in on the male-enhancement gold rush, and who sells his wares as an antidote to all the cosmetic procedures women can get to feel better about themselves. His massive house and impressive car collection speak more plainly to his motives in this space than his riffs to customers about self-esteem or the blarney about posting their post-op results on his company website.

Moore’s company PhalloFill, which specializes in “girth enhancement”, has expanded to 32 locations across the country. He hopes to make the procedure as common as Botox. “Bill tried to get me to have my penis enlarged,” says Lombroso. The thought never occurred. “I said my mom would never forgive me.”

But the great shame in Manhood isn’t that Moore and other practitioners in this charcoal gray area of medicine lavish their customers with patience and empathy. It’s that few see the tender treatment for what it is: gender-affirming care. “That’s why this movie has a very light touch,” Lombroso says. “So many of these things are funny and self-evident, especially to smart viewers. It’s fun to have these tough conversations and not tell people exactly how to feel in every moment.”

Manhood is now playing in select US cinemas with UK and Australia dates to be announced

article_text:
Chi l’ha proferita l’ultima parola sulla “morte della pittura”? Negli atelier di tutta Italia, una wave di giovani artisti sta dimostrando l’esatto contrario, innestando la tradizione classica all’immaginario iper-connesso dei nostri giorni. Questa nuova rubrica è dedicata ai pittori emergenti attivi nel Bel Paese. Attraverso interviste dirette e senza filtri dietro le quinte della loro ricerca, andiamo a scoprire le ossessioni, gli sconfinamenti linguistici di chi ha scelto il medium più antico del mondo per raccontare la complessità del presente, nel solco di una ridefinizione dei generi tradizionali, dal ritratto al paesaggio e alla natura morta. Abbiamo incontrato Alessandro Miotti (Marostica, 1991), qui la nostra intervista.

Come descriveresti oggi, in poche righe, la tua ricerca pittorica?

«La mia è una ricerca autoanalitica che dialoga con la memoria collettiva. Metto in evidenza soggetti come l’animale e il cowboy, insieme al contenuto emotivo che ne deriva, collocandoli in scenari prevalentemente bucolici e onirici.»

Come ti sei avvicinato alla pittura?

«Il primo giorno in cui sono entrato all’Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia mi sono stupito nello scoprire che esistevano, nel contemporaneo, persone che facevano della pittura la propria vita. Così ho deciso di provarci anch’io.»

Quali sono gli artisti e maestri del passato che senti come riferimenti o punti di ispirazione? E tra i contemporanei, chi segui con maggiore interesse?

«La lista cambia nel corso degli anni. Nutro una profonda ammirazione per Goya e ho realizzato alcuni dipinti che sono esplicite citazioni del suo lavoro. In questo momento mi sono avvicinato molto a Bacon e Ligabue, ma continuo a fare molta ricerca. Tra i pittori contemporanei che seguo con interesse, per fare un paio di nomi, citerei Seth Becker e Travis MacDonald.»

La pittura per te è un fine o un mezzo?

«Entrambe le cose. La mia ricerca prova a dare una chiave pop alla pittura, idealmente fruibile da chiunque: il fine è che tutti possano comprenderla, mentre il mezzo per arrivarci è la pratica artistica.»

Quali temi affronti nel tuo lavoro e perché li ritieni importanti in questo momento?

«Il mio lavoro parla di istinto e solitudine, di bisogni primari e questioni identitarie che riguardano tutti. Utilizzo il cliché come strumento per costruire immagini immediate, capaci di suggerire una narrazione emotiva attraverso l’impatto visivo e la prima sensazione, evocando immaginari condivisi o ricordi personali.»

Quali elementi consideri fondamentali nel tuo modo di dipingere (ad esempio colore, segno, composizione, materia, tecnica)?

«La materia, il segno e un intenso lavoro di sovrapposizione pittorica, attraverso cui cerco di restituire gli aspetti più significativi della costruzione del dipinto. Questo processo comprende passaggi ad acrilico, pastelli a olio, spray e pittura a olio.»

Quanto influisce il contesto contemporaneo (sociale, culturale o politico) sul tuo lavoro?

«Sono inevitabilmente influenzato da ciò che accade oggi sul piano politico e sociale, e mi sento coinvolto. Viviamo immersi in un flusso continuo di notizie e disinformazione, spesso difficile da decifrare. Nel confronto con la realtà veneziana in cui vivo e con le storie che ascolto, raccolgo inquietudini e contraddizioni che sento il bisogno di elaborare attraverso il mio lavoro. Le serie di dipinti cercano di sollevare domande su temi come la guerra, l’identità e il bisogno di sentirsi accettati.»

Utilizzi strumenti digitali o intelligenza artificiale nel tuo processo creativo? Se sì, in che modo?

«No.»

Quali influssi esterni alla pittura (per esempio cinema, musica, letteratura, immagini online, ecc.) sono più presenti nel tuo lavoro?

«Ascolto molta musica e negli ultimi anni mi sono avvicinato particolarmente al rap, frequentandone anche l’ambiente. Per me è diventato un riferimento importante, perché credo sia un genere musicale che parte dal basso, capace di portare alla luce problematiche della vita quotidiana e della strada, attraverso una spinta comunicativa di denuncia sociale. Per certi aspetti, anche il mio lavoro pittorico, o il modo in cui lo svolgo, si avvicina a questo approccio. Cerco inoltre di mantenermi stimolato attraverso il cinema e, soprattutto, la lettura. Leggere è un esercizio quotidiano che considero fondamentale per alimentare e approfondire la mia ricerca pittorica.»

Nel tuo lavoro quanto spazio hanno l’esperienza personale e quella collettiva?

«Come dicevo descrivendo il mio lavoro, l’intento è quello di condividere un’esperienza collettiva, cercando di ricreare immagini riconoscibili a tutti, almeno nei loro valori emotivi. Queste immagini derivano dalla mia esperienza personale e dall’osservazione di ciò che mi circonda, nel tentativo di trovare un punto d’incontro tra la dimensione individuale e quella collettiva.»

Durante la realizzazione di un’opera, qual è il momento che consideri più importante e come incide sul risultato finale?

«Uno dei momenti più importanti è l’abbozzo dell’immagine, che incide profondamente sulla freschezza e sulla tensione del quadro. Per me è un passaggio cruciale, durante il quale si stabiliscono le principali gerarchie focali dell’opera, determinando buona parte del risultato finale.»

Quando decidi che un’opera è conclusa?

«Ogni volta è un po’ diverso. A volte ho la sensazione che alcuni lavori mi portino allo sfinimento; altre volte mi fermo quando sento di non riuscire a dare un ulteriore contributo qualitativo e mi accorgo che il dipinto, nonostante continui a lavorarci, non cambia più. In altri casi, molto più rari, lo guardo e semplicemente dico: basta.»

Cosa ti porta a scegliere la pittura oggi, nel contesto contemporaneo?

«Più che una scelta di convenienza, mi sembra una questione di predisposizione, non tanto innata quanto coltivata attraverso il tempo, il lavoro e la fatica. Penso che questo valga per tutte le pratiche artistiche: il fatto stesso che continuino a emergere e non vadano perdute nel tempo ne determina l’esistenza. Per questo motivo direi che, nel contemporaneo, la pittura è ancora viva.»

Pensi che il valore della tua opera possa variare all’interno di una grande mostra collettiva come Ensemble ? In che modo?

«Non credo che il valore di un’opera cambi in base al contesto in cui viene esposta. All’interno di una mostra collettiva, però, può assumere significati e letture differenti, entrando in dialogo con gli altri lavori e dando vita a relazioni che, isolatamente, non emergerebbero.»

article_text:
James Gunn continues building out the DC Universe and recently questioned Margot Robbie ‘s involvement as Harley Quinn.

The DC Studios co-head released a podcast titled The Suicide Squad : Is It Canon ? where he answered fan questions about which characters would transfer to his new universe.

When Robbie’s Harley Quinn came up, Gunn said, “I think Harley is actually one of the more difficult things in this to justify as being canon in the DCU.”

Gunn pointed out that the relationship between Harley and the Joker is very specific, and the Joker hasn’t been established in the DCU yet. The filmmaker reminded viewers that only Batman has been established in his cameo on the animated series Creature Commandos .

Related Stories

James Gunn Claps Back At Critics Of Continuity In His DCU

'Clayface' Director James Watkins Explains Aaron Paul's Cameo: "A Real Brief Easter Egg"

Reminiscing about the time he spent directing Margot Robbie in 2021’s The Suicide Squad , Gunn said Robbie “is one of my favorite actors to work with,” adding, “She is so good in the movie. I love her as Harley.”

Watch on Deadline

“I don’t know if she wants to play Harley again. She may be over that,” Gunn said.

Podcast co-host Jennifer Holland pointed out that Robbie has become even a bigger star since filming The Suicide Squad . However, Gunn said Robbie can return as Harley Quinn if she decides to.

“I don’t know where Margot’s head is with all of this,” he said. “Harley is a character I’m almost certainly going to use in the DCU, and if Margot wants to play her, then I’ll bend over backwards to explain that in the world. But if she doesn’t, then I might go with somebody else, where I don’t have to be attached to what happens to Harley in this movie.”

Robbie first played Harley Quinn in 2016’s Suicide Squad and reprised the role in 2020’s Birds of Prey . When Gunn took over the villainous characters for 2021’s The Suicide Squad , Quinn also returned.

Between Sound and Light: Yoshikatsu Ikeuchi’s “Liminal”

YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI ,

Elusive , 2026, oil on canvas, 53 x 45.5 cm. Courtesy the artist.

Yoshikatsu Ikeuchi Liminal Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art October 13–25, 2026

Rather than staging a dialogue in which painting and sound mutually illuminate each other, Japanese artist Yoshikatsu Ikeuchi’s “Liminal,” which ran at the Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art this October, was built around what cannot be exchanged between them, the irreducible differences that persist when one form of expression attempts to become another.

Ikeuchi was born in Kyoto and grew up in a household where painting and composing were routine parts of daily life. He began releasing his own compositions online while still in high school. His practice has since become a sustained investigation of how expression changes shape when it moves between forms.

YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI ’s “Liminal” at Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art, 2026. Courtesy Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art.

Installation view of YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI ’s “Liminal” at Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art, 2026. Courtesy Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art.

YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI ’s “Liminal” at Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art, 2026. Courtesy Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art.

Between Forms

“Liminal” brought together 23 oil paintings, drawings, three sculptures, and a sound installation, displayed in a museum space with a glass ceiling 14 metres overhead. Natural light shifted across the works through the day, and with no fixed route through the space, each visitor’s experience depended on where they stood, what they encountered first, and what time they arrived.

The sound installation 47, 61, 73, (2026) was what most visitors encountered first. Three organic tones emanated from an unseen source above the entrance, cycling at intervals of 47, 61, and 73 seconds respectively. Since the three numbers share no common factors, their relationship at any given moment is determined entirely by where they happen to be in their independent cycles. Full convergence occurs only once every 58 hours. The piece doesn’t so much repeat as continuously rearrange itself, which turns duration, how long you spend in the space and which path you take through it, into part of the compositional material.

YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI ,

Remnant of Light , 2026, oil on canvas, 53 x 45.5 cm. Courtesy the artist.

YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI ,

Unbecoming Self , 2026, oil on canvas, 80 x 65 cm. Courtesy the artist.

Soft Worlds

Pale and layered, inhabited by solitary figures and strange creatures rendered in a flattened graphic style reminiscent of animation, Ikeuchi’s paintings activate recognizable cultural associations, childhood, innocence, the pastoral. Yet, they are also distorted just enough to stop those associations from settling. Outlines do not quite align. Expressions are hard to read. Bodies are mid-transformation.

Remnant of Light (2026) depicts a child seated on a wooden crate in a pale meadow, the childʼs head enclosed in a translucent sphere, like a soap bubble or a diverʼs helmet, that slightly distorts the features within. The expression, insofar as it registers, suggests a kind of distracted indifference. Scattered across the grass are smaller spheres, identical in form to the one around the childʼs head, lying loose across the meadow, unattached to anyone. It is unclear whether they have been shed or were never inhabited. While the repetition of spheres creates a visual rhyme between the figures and the surrounding landscape, the role played by these translucent forms shifts from instance to instance, resisting any reduction to a single, fixed interpretation. Another work, Unbecoming Self (2026), features a girl pulling a creature from a body of water, a solitary house and forested hills behind her. The background evokes the tonal warmth of illustrated children’s fiction while the creature, with its blunt simplicity, generates a sense of unease.

YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI ,

ZENTEI , 2026, oil on canvas, 130.3 x 162 cm. Courtesy the artist.

Modest in scale and quiet in sensibility, Elusive (2026) depicts a girl looking outward against a soft blue ground. Her eyes hold tears, gathered but not yet falling. She gazes directly out of the canvas, placing the viewer in the position of someone being looked at. The expression in her brows and the set of her mouth is level, not grief-configured, as if she is observing. In reading such an expression as “sadness,” Ikeuchi suggests, something is also lost, the particular quality of a gaze, a complicated, layered emotional charge, and an atmosphere that the word cannot fully hold.

YOSHIKATSU IKEUCHI . Courtesy the artist.

About the artist

Based in Tokyo and born in Kyoto, Ikeuchi is an artist and composer whose practice moves between sound, installation, and painting. In 2016, he scored Lee Sang-il’s psychologically dense film Rage ( Ikari ), working under Ryuichi Sakamoto’s musical direction.

Ikeuchi was recently appointed Honorary Cultural Ambassador for Kyoto Prefecture by the Governor, a role centered on sharing the prefecture’s creative culture internationally. His recent solo exhibitions include “MUSORY” at the Kyoto National Museum (November 2025) and “Liminal” at the Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art (October 2026). “Liminal” was presented as an initiative to spotlight new forms of culture emerging from Kyoto; the exhibition drew 12,826 visitors over its 12 opening days.

In addition, a collaboration between Yoshikatsu Ikeuchi and BE@RBRICK was announced at “Liminal,” with pre-orders opening during the exhibition run. A collaboration with wine glass brand RIEDEL was also unveiled at the exhibition. Products will go on sale in 2027 at RIEDEL stores and through its online shop.

article_text:
The Seoul Museum of Art has appointed Irini Papadimitriou as Artistic Director of the 14th Seoul Mediacity Biennale, following an international open call.

Papadimitriou is currently Director of Exhibitions at Diriyah Art Futures in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and has previously held UK roles at V&A in London and FutureEverything in Manchester.

Under the theme ‘Machines of Repair’, the Biennale aims to ‘create a space for fundamental reflection on the values and purposes that scientific and technological progress and innovation ultimately serve’, according to the Museum’s announcement.

‘At a time when technological innovation is too often driven by conquest, extraction, surveillance, and control, I look forward to building on the Seoul Mediacity Biennale’s legacy of bringing art and emerging technologies into critical dialogue,’ Papadimitriou said in a statement. ‘The 14th Biennale will critically examine how these systems shape our societies and futures. Beyond exposing these realities, my vision is to open up a space for collective imagination and dialogue, asking how technology might be reoriented towards infrastructures of the public good.’

The fourteenth edition is due to open in August 2027.

The previous edition of the Seoul Mediacity Biennale, titled Séance: Technology of the Spirit , opened in 2025 and was curated by Anton Vidokle, Hallie Ayres and Lukas Brasiskis.

Der Arthouse-Streamingdienst beteiligt sich im Oktober mit „The Faust Bible“ an einer aufwändigen Buchpublikation und zeigt passend dazu Murnaus „Faust“-Stummfilm sowie weitere Verfilmungen deutschsprachiger Literatur. Sandra Hüller darf zum MUBI-Start von „Rose“ fünf Filme aus dessen Programm hervorheben. Zudem startet „Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma“ und wird von weiteren ambitionierten Horrorfilmen begleitet.

Im Oktober blickt der Arthouse-Streamingdienst auf ein hundertjähriges Jubiläum. Am 14. Oktober 1926 hatte einer der berühmtesten deutschen Stummfilme seine Uraufführung: F.W. Murnaus „ Faust “-Verfilmung, die mit enormem Aufwand die Legende um den Gelehrten erzählt, der von Mephisto als Gesandtem des Teufels zu einem Pakt verführt wird, dessen Einsatz Fausts Seele ist. Der Film emanzipierte sich mit dem Zusatztitel „Eine deutsche Volkssage“ auch von einer allzu dichten Bindung an Goethes berühmte Theaterstücke und setzt mit Bildgewalt, Licht- und Schattenspiel und dem groß aufspielenden Emil Jannings als Mephisto auf die spielerische Freude am Phantastischen. Murnaus Kameramann Carl Hoffmann sowie die Szenen- und Kostümbildner Robert Herlth und Walter Röhrig dokumentierten seinerzeit die Entstehung des Films und verehrten dem Regisseur zum Abschluss die rund 400 Fotografien und Illustrationen.

Lange verschollen, wurde das Material ab 2017 von der Cinémathèque française restauriert und erscheint nun am 17. Oktober als edle Publikation unter dem Titel „The Faust Bible“ bei MUBI Editions. Zur Feier des Buchs nimmt der Streamingdienst schon am 9. Oktober Murnaus Stummfilm-Klassiker ins Programm auf. Flankiert wird er von weiteren deutschsprachigen Literaturverfilmungen, darunter „ Metropolis “, „ Der blaue Engel “ und „ Die Blechtrommel “.

Meta-Horror und Verkleidung im 17. Jahrhundert

Geht es bei „Faust“ schon mitunter gruselig zu, hat MUBI im Oktober auch für Halloween-Fans wieder härtere Horror-Kost im Angebot. Am 2. Oktober feiert „ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma “ Premiere bei dem Streamingdienst, der zu den meistbeachteten Filmen beim Festival in Cannes 2026 gehörte und dort die Reihe „Un certain regard“ eröffnete. Der Meta-Horrorfilm kreist um eine queere Filmemacherin, die einer angestaubten Slasher-Reihe neues Leben einhauen will, ohne dabei deren regressive Geschlechterbilder zu verwenden. Neben dem Film von Jane Schoenbrun präsentiert MUBI in der sogenannten „Dusk Till Dawn: Die Camp-Miasma-Halloween-Sleepover-Sammlung“ schon ab 1. Oktober Filme von John Carpenter , David Cronenberg und Na Hong-jin sowie als Geheimtipp das spanische Horror-Experiment „ Arrebato “ von 1979.

Nur unter historischem Blickwinkel unheimlich, in der Form aber ein konzentriertes, einfühlsames und sogar lyrisches Historiendrama ist die zweite prominente MUBI-Premiere des Oktobers: „ Rose “ des österreichischen Filmemachers Markus Schleinzer handelt von einem Soldaten, der während des Dreißigjährigen Krieges in einem Dorf Anspruch auf einen verwaisten Gutshof erhebt. Hinter dem Fremden verbirgt sich eine Frau, die sich als Mann ausgibt, und ihr Geheimnis nicht ewig verbergen kann. Das Drama brachte Hauptdarstellerin Sandra Hüller einmal mehr viel Anerkennung und den Schauspielpreis auf der Berlinale ein. Für MUBI hat Hüller nun fünf Werke ausgewählt, die zum Start von „Rose“ am 16. Oktober ebenfalls präsentiert werden. Neben Chantal Akermans feministischem Klassiker „ Jeanne Dielman “ gehören dazu „ Gesetz und Ordnung “ von Frederick Wiseman, der Kurzfilm „ Four Roads “ von Alice Rohrwacher, „ Aftersun “ von Charlotte Wells und „ The Mastermind “ von Kelly Reichardt.

Entdeckung aus Cornwall

Mit dem Regisseur Mark Jenkin stellt MUBI im Oktober auch einen Filmschaffenden vor, dessen Bekanntheit sich bislang vor allem auf Kurzfilm-Festivals und sein Spielfilmdebüt „ Bait “ (2019) beschränkt. Ab 16. Oktober sind sechs Kurzfilme des Filmemachers aus Cornwall zu sehen, die allesamt mit seiner Heimat verbunden sind und in ihrer Ästhetik die strengen Regeln seines 2013 publizierten Manifests „ Silent Landscape Dancing Grain 13 “ befolgen. Wie in „Bait“ verbinden sich auch in Jenkins Kurzfilmen Archaik und Gegenwart zu poetischen Erzählungen, die von der kornischen Landschaft inspiriert sind.

Images of a shrinking glacier in Iceland and a Ukrainian Saturday School in Scotland have been announced as the gold and silver winners of the AOP’s 2026 Emerging Talent Awards, celebrating the very best in the new wave of photographers and image makers, who have been practising their craft for less than three years. With no restrictions on what can be entered and open to AOP members and non-members alike, through this award the AOP provides a chance for emerging photographers and image makers to be seen by leading commissioners and names within the photographic industry."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "15 individual finalists’ works were shortlisted for the 2026 AOP Emerging Talent Award, all of which can be seen here :"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "https://www.aopawards.com/finalists-gallery-emerging-talent-2026/", "links": [{"text": "https://www.aopawards.com/finalists-gallery-emerging-talent-2026/", "url": "https://www.aopawards.com/finalists-gallery-emerging-talent-2026/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Austin Bradley (UK graduate, 2025) has been awarded gold for his work, 57 Metres: Iceland’s Shrinking Glacier. With climate change becoming hard to understand through anonymous statistics and figures, Bradley wanted to find a way to visually communicate glacial retreat. In response to this he rigged a 57-metre highline across Sólheimajökull Glacier in Iceland, with the length of the line representing approximately how far the glacier retreats each year due to a warming climate. Over several carbon offset days Bradley worked with highliners, a small film crew and a glaciologist, to document the process, which will later be released as a documentary."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026 Judge, Jack Eames, himself an award-winning AOP Accredited Photographer, says of the work, “I fell in love with these images as soon as I saw them – a fantastic execution of a really important concept, with incredible depth and texture, and a really visceral sense of scale both metaphorically and physically.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ritchie Elder’s series Saturday School won the silver prize for the AOP’s 2026 Emerging Talent Awards, documenting the final day of the school term at the Ukrainian Saturday School at Leith Academy. Established more than three years ago, the school is the first of its kind in Scotland. It provides Ukrainian children displaced by the war with the opportunity to learn Ukrainian language, culture, and history alongside their mainstream education and plays an important role in helping young people maintain a connection to their heritage while building new lives in Scotland. Elder worked closely with the children, their parents, and school staff to create this series. Saturday School forms part of a wider documentary project developed in collaboration with the Association of Ukrainians in Great Britain, documenting Ukrainian culture and community life across Scotland."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kim Pappas, Agent, Process and 2026 Judge, says of the work, “There is a real tenderness to the Saturday School portraits, and the way the light falls on the young subjects is beautiful. A good portrait is emotive and moving – and I think this series touched us all.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Emerging Talent Award reflects the AOP’s commitment to supporting photographers at every stage of their career. article_text:
Winners Announced for the 2026 AOP Emerging Talent Award . Images of a shrinking glacier in Iceland and a Ukrainian Saturday School in Scotland have been announced as the gold and silver winners of the AOP’s 2026 Emerging Talent Awards, celebrating the very best in the new wave of photographers and image makers, who have been practising their craft for less than three years. With no restrictions on what can be entered and open to AOP members and non-members alike, through this award the AOP provides a chance for emerging photographers and image makers to be seen by leading commissioners and names within the photographic industry.

15 individual finalists’ works were shortlisted for the 2026 AOP Emerging Talent Award, all of which can be seen here :

https://www.aopawards.com/finalists-gallery-emerging-talent-2026/

Austin Bradley (UK graduate, 2025) has been awarded gold for his work, 57 Metres: Iceland’s Shrinking Glacier. With climate change becoming hard to understand through anonymous statistics and figures, Bradley wanted to find a way to visually communicate glacial retreat. In response to this he rigged a 57-metre highline across Sólheimajökull Glacier in Iceland, with the length of the line representing approximately how far the glacier retreats each year due to a warming climate. Over several carbon offset days Bradley worked with highliners, a small film crew and a glaciologist, to document the process, which will later be released as a documentary.

2026 Judge, Jack Eames, himself an award-winning AOP Accredited Photographer, says of the work, “I fell in love with these images as soon as I saw them – a fantastic execution of a really important concept, with incredible depth and texture, and a really visceral sense of scale both metaphorically and physically.”

Ritchie Elder’s series Saturday School won the silver prize for the AOP’s 2026 Emerging Talent Awards, documenting the final day of the school term at the Ukrainian Saturday School at Leith Academy. Established more than three years ago, the school is the first of its kind in Scotland. It provides Ukrainian children displaced by the war with the opportunity to learn Ukrainian language, culture, and history alongside their mainstream education and plays an important role in helping young people maintain a connection to their heritage while building new lives in Scotland. Elder worked closely with the children, their parents, and school staff to create this series. Saturday School forms part of a wider documentary project developed in collaboration with the Association of Ukrainians in Great Britain, documenting Ukrainian culture and community life across Scotland.

Kim Pappas, Agent, Process and 2026 Judge, says of the work, “There is a real tenderness to the Saturday School portraits, and the way the light falls on the young subjects is beautiful. A good portrait is emotive and moving – and I think this series touched us all.”

The Emerging Talent Award reflects the AOP’s commitment to supporting photographers at every stage of their career. A popular competition, it attracts entries globally and with no categories or themes in this competition, the choice of work submitted is entirely up to the photographer and can be personal or commissioned. As in previous years, stills, moving image, and the creative use of technologies and innovations in the production of works created by a person are accepted, although AI-produced images are not. All images must have been created on or after 1 January 2025.

The four judges for the 2026 AOP Emerging Talent Awards are:

Jack Eames, Award-winning AOP Accredited Photographer

Jason Baron, Creative Consultant and recent Head of Photo/Video, BUILDHOLLYWOOD

Kate Congreve, Producer, Mother London

Kim Pappas, Agent, Process

Isabelle Doran, CEO of the Association of Photographers, says of the 2026 AOP Emerging Talent Award, “This year’s prevailing genre shining through both still and moving image submissions is undoubtedly human-focused, even where the human imprint is on places and animals. It’s an impressive selection of work, chosen by our expert panel of judges, for our 2026 Emerging Talent finalists, and I’m looking forward to seeing their career development with anticipation.”

Sponsored by BUILDHOLLYWOOD, the Gold-winning work by Austin Bradley will be exhibited from 19th–25th October 2026 across selected BUILDHOLLYWOOD digital sites throughout London, creating a street gallery for the work across the city. In addition, co-sponsor Wex Photo Video will exhibit all finalists’ work onsite at their Putney store location in London. Gold and Silver winners will be announced live on the evening of 14 October 2026 at the exhibition Private View. Prizes include a tailored AOP Associate Membership Package designed with the recipient’s career path in mind, along with advice on advancing their current professional photography practice which includes a 1:1 Folio Review with industry representatives; and a Business Practice Review worth £500.

Khaly Nguyen, Marketing Director, BUILDHOLLYWOOD, says of the Award, “Emerging photographers bring fresh perspectives and new ways of seeing the world. At BUILDHOLLYWOOD, we’re proud to support the AOP Emerging Talent Award and give the next generation of creative voices a platform on the streets. Austin Bradley’s winning entry is a brilliant example of the ambition, originality and passion for causes that matter coming through in this new wave of image-makers. We can’t wait to see his photography displayed on our sites, creating a street gallery across London.”

Mark Baber, Head of Events, Wex Photo Video, explains, “Supporting emerging talent is something we feel strongly about at Wex Photo Video, and we’re delighted to support the AOP Emerging Talent Awards. This year’s shortlist shows the creativity, fresh ideas and powerful storytelling coming into our industry. Through our retail stores, knowledgeable staff and our events programme, we help photographers build confidence, develop their skills and find the right equipment to bring their ideas to life. Congratulations to the winners and all the finalists. There’s a lot to be proud of, and we look forward to seeing what you create next.”

Jason Baron, Creative Consultant and 2026 Judge, says “Every year I judge an emerging artist award the quality is always high. This year is no different. The images and projects that stood out for me were the ones where people had avoided the usual cliches and tropes of ‘award-winning’ photography. Established photographers should quite rightly be slightly quaking in their boots at the younger ones coming through. Then everyone has to work harder to think differently and move things forward.”

The many awards presented by the AOP in its calendar reflect the organisation’s commitment to showcasing the very best in photography, as well as promoting and protecting the rights of professional photographers at all stages in their career and celebrating the diversity of creative human endeavour.

title_original: Interview: Hlynur Pálmason on The Love That Remains
editorial_title_zh: 访谈：赫林古·帕尔马松谈《The Love That Remains》
editorial_excerpt_zh: 家庭空间：这位冰岛作者导演探讨了他最新的亲密史诗作品，影片讲述了一对分居的夫妇在婚姻之外的生活中共同抚育孩子的故事
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "自冰岛导演赫林古·帕尔马松（Hlynur Pálmason）2017年的导演处女作《冬兄弟》问世以来，他已证明自己是一位风格独特且多产的作者导演——涉足从社会剧到爱情片、警匪片到历史史诗等广泛的类型常规，同时发展出鲜明的风格以及对时间本质的关注。他迄今为止执导的四部剧情长片都带有他标志性的延时摄影序列：他将摄像机固定在一个观察点上，有时会长达数月之久，然后将所拍摄的影像浓缩成震撼的蒙太奇，以此反思荒凉的冰岛乡村与季节的更替。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在2022年的突破之作《上帝之地》之后，外界的期待值非常高。这部宏大的作品探讨了19世纪冰岛的丹麦殖民主义与基督教，曾在戛纳电影节“一种关注”单元首映并获得国际赞誉。他决定用一部像《The Love That Remains》这样亲密、克制且带着依恋的作品来紧随这样一部宏大的作品，这或许会让人感到意外，但也仅仅是乍看之下如此。《The Love That Remains》讲述了安娜（Saga Garðarsdóttir饰）和马格努斯（Sverrir Gudnason饰）的生活，这是一对最近分居的夫妇，在婚姻之外的生活中共同抚育他们的三个孩子。影片本身就是一部史诗——一曲对挥之不去的情感、爱意可以呈现的多种形态，以及艺术和梦想在我们日常生活中所扮演角色的深情赞歌。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在布加勒斯特戛纳电影节（Les Films de Cannes à Bucarest）上采访了帕尔马松。这是一个由金棕榈奖得主克里斯蒂安·蒙吉u（Cristian Mungiu）创立的戛纳集锦年度回顾展，去年曾举办过一个聚焦帕尔马松电影的小型专题展。我们讨论了他的电影标志和开放式的工作流程，以及克劳德·莫奈（Claude Monet）和欧仁·德拉克罗瓦（Eugène Delacroix）等经典画家对他的艺术技巧和世界观的影响。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "看到你从像《上帝之地》这样的电影转向如此亲密的作品，让人感到意外。你在2022年的短片《Nest》中就显露过你在筹备这样一部电影的迹象，该片讲述了三个兄妹——由你自己的孩子扮演，他们也出演了《The Love That Remains》——历时一年建造一座树屋的故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Nest》促使我开始认真将《The Love That Remains》作为我的下一个项目来对待。因为我花了两年时间拍摄我的孩子和这座树屋，我在一个小棚子里度过了很长时间，读书或者等待动物进入画幅。当我坐在那里的时候，我开始思考：这些孩子的父母在做什么？于是，我开始为他们写一个小故事。不过，我们为《The Love That Remains》拍摄的第一组镜头是在2017年——也就是开场时那座打开的屋顶的画面。那是在《上帝之地》之前。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我们把家从丹麦搬到冰岛乡村时，我们买了自己的电影摄影机和配件。我每天都把摄像机放在车里，随心所欲地拍摄任何我想拍的东西。这就是我构建和创作电影的方式——使用我早已拍好的素材，而不是把整部剧本写完。我一直在拍摄然后做出反应，而这些素材决定了我前进的方向。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《The Love That Remains》中对男子气概有一种带有戏谑意味的批判，它延续了《上帝之地》中探讨的相似主题，但方式非常不同。例如，其中有一个非常美好的场景，马格努斯抬头看安娜的裙底，你在其中玩味了男性凝视的概念。在大多数电影中，这个场景会显得有些猥琐，但你把它转化成了一个如此温柔且充满爱意的时刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一个男性，我对外在的这些事物很着迷——这些基本的、原始的需求和欲望。我记得在早期拍摄掀裙子那场戏时，团队里有人说这可能会被负面解读。这取决于你如何去拍。如果它是带着对美的天真喜悦来拍的，那么它就会以那种方式表达出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的电影有着非常鲜明的个人印记：你曾将延时摄影序列用在《白日郎郎》（2019）的开场镜头中、《上帝之地》的片尾序列中，甚至作为《Nest》整部电影的结构。在《The Love That Remains》中，这些场景散布在整部电影中，感觉更加具有自我意识和解构色彩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我对季节和天气的脾性非常感兴趣：它们的美丽与残酷、冷暖的对比、静止与风暴。我几乎把它们当作绘画的调色板来平衡电影。如果电影中出现了一段艰难的时期——例如在《The Love That Remains》中，当关系开始变得暴力或危险，或者当感情开始变质时——我就可以用那些能够提升这些情绪的画面。我把它们当作电影中的情感色彩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当你观看一部电影并能感受到时间的流逝时，对我和观众来说，电影就变得更加真实了。这就像看着某样东西生长。这是非常情绪化的。我仍在探索中。我认为下一部电影将是极致的，就像完全沉浸在时间和空间中一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些场景让我想起了莫奈的作品，尤其是他在花园中的探索。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这与莫奈有很多相通之处。我记得自己曾深受德拉克罗瓦和保罗·克利（Paul Klee）的画作与日记，以及丹麦画家佩尔·柯克比（Per Kirkeby）的大量文字所启发。还有一个来自加泰罗尼亚的西班牙人[安东尼]·塔皮埃斯（Antoni Tàpies），他写过两本回忆录。当我读了这些书然后看到他们的画作时，我被他们所描绘的极其平凡的事物深深打动了——比如他们只是在画自己的孩子洗澡、他们周末要吃的食物，或者一瓶葡萄酒。我被它们在情感上所激发。我觉得这很美，这与生活的起伏息息相关。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我读他们的日记时，发现它们也非常普通、接地气。“好吧，我还剩多少钱买吃的？我有多少钱买颜料？我要买什么颜色的？外面的天气怎么样？冷吗？我的身体怎么样？我感觉怎么样？”我能对这些事情产生共鸣，因为这表明，作为人类，我们其实并没有变多少。无论是德拉克洛瓦的时代还是今天，我们都是一样的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的孩子们在创作他们自己的场景方面参与了多少？这部电影借鉴了很多孩子们的幽默，而且非常真实，极其符合童年的真实感受。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果某种东西非常自由，那么你就会分不清它是即兴创作还是精心构建的。我是约翰·卡萨维茨（John Cassavetes）的超级粉丝。他拍电影的方式赋予了[它们]一种奇异的现实感。他有着漫长的写作、排练和测试剧本的过程。这就是他构建这种即兴感的方式，好让电影感觉新鲜、真实。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我经常思考这一点，并努力让我的电影感觉真实，尤其是因为镜头并不是手持的。有时会有些摇镜头，但没有轨道车（dolly），什么都没有。它极其简单且接地气。我们在让对话显得流畅方面做了大量工作。例如，对于孩子们，我会为他们写一个场景。然后我会把这个场景交给我最大的女儿。她和几个男孩一起琢磨。他们进行了测试。后来，当我在做晚饭时，他们过来把场景表演了一遍。接着我可能会提点意见，或者稍微重写一下，或者他们提出了想法，然后突然之间效果就更好了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但剧本、用于主体拍摄的最终拍摄剧本极其详细。每一个停顿、每一个逗号，一切都在那儿。而且他们真的很擅长拿捏，哪怕我们拍了第三次、第四次甚至20次，他们也真的很擅长一次又一次地做出相同的反应。还有一些时候，我试图捕捉某人脸红或对某事做出反应的瞬间，而他们可能并不知道我在拍他们。我这么做是因为我知道电影里有些东西是装不出来的，或者装出来根本就很无聊。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的孩子们看过这部电影吗？他们感觉如何？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他们在戛纳看了这部电影，并且非常喜欢。这其实是首映礼上最美好的事情之一——在观影时听到他们放声大笑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "显然，我为他们在电影中的表现感到非常骄傲。但我也很高兴这并没有让他们感到困惑。因为他们对成为演员、电影人或艺术家并不感兴趣。我觉得这种态度在银幕上非常好。他们根本不在乎。他们这么做是为了我。为了好玩，为了成为团队的一部分。还有为了拿报酬。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你接下来在筹备什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在，我们正在制作一部古装片。它讲的是我现在的居所、我的家乡赫本（Höfn）的起源。它取材于一位名叫奥托·图利纽斯（Ottó Tuliníus）的商人的生平，他曾住在小镇所在山脉的另一侧。故事讲述了他和家人拆掉自己的房子，把它变成一个木筏，把所有的东西都搬上去，然后从海路绕过这座山，去寻找重建房子的新地方。我已经断断续续地筹备和拍摄了一年，接下来还要拍两年。从某种意义上说，这也是一部像《巢》那样的作品，但被推向了极致：这是我拍过最极致、最奇怪的电影。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Since Hlynur Pálmason’s 2017 debut feature Winter Brothers , the Icelandic director has proven himself to be an idiosyncratic and versatile auteur—dabbling in a wide range of genre conventions from social drama to romance, policier to historical epic—while also developing a distinctive style and preoccupation with the nature of time. The four features he has made so far each feature his signature time-lapse sequences: he places his camera at a static point of observation, sometimes for months on end, then condenses the resulting images into arresting montages that reflect on the stark Icelandic countryside and the passage of the seasons."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Expectations were high after 2022’s breakout Godland , a sprawling exploration of Danish colonialism and Christianity in 19th-century Iceland, which premiered to international acclaim in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival. His decision to follow such an ambitious work with something as intimate, restrained, and wistful as The Love That Remains may come as a surprise, but only at first glance. Following the lives of Anna (Saga Garðarsdóttir) and Magnús (Sverrir Gudnason), a recently separated couple co-parenting their three children while navigating life beyond marriage, The Love That Remains is an epic in its own right—a deeply poetic homage to lingering feelings, the many shapes affection can take, and the role that art and dreams play in our everyday lives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I caught up with Pálmason at Les Films de Cannes à Bucarest, a yearly retrospective of the highlights of Cannes founded by Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, which last year presented a small focus on Pálmason’s films. We discussed his cinematic signatures and open-ended working process, and the influence of canonical painters such as Claude Monet and Eugène Delacroix on his artistic techniques and worldview."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s surprising to see you go from a film like Godland to something that’s so much more intimate. There were hints that you were working on a film like this in your 2022 short, Nest, which follows three siblings—played by your own kids, who also appear in The Love That Remains —building a tree house over the course of a year."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nest prompted me to begin taking The Love That Remains seriously as my next project. Because I spent two years filming my kids and this tree house, I spent much time inside a small shed, reading books or waiting for animals to come into the frame. And while I sat there, I started thinking: what are the parents of these children doing? So, I started writing a small narrative for them. However, the first thing that we shot for The Love That Remains was in 2017—the image of the roof that opens the movie. That was before Godland ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When we moved our family from Denmark to the countryside of Iceland, we bought our own film camera and accessories. I just keep the camera in the car every day and film whatever I want. This is how I construct and build my films—using the material I’ve already shot instead of writing the whole thing. article_text:
Since Hlynur Pálmason’s 2017 debut feature Winter Brothers , the Icelandic director has proven himself to be an idiosyncratic and versatile auteur—dabbling in a wide range of genre conventions from social drama to romance, policier to historical epic—while also developing a distinctive style and preoccupation with the nature of time. The four features he has made so far each feature his signature time-lapse sequences: he places his camera at a static point of observation, sometimes for months on end, then condenses the resulting images into arresting montages that reflect on the stark Icelandic countryside and the passage of the seasons.

Expectations were high after 2022’s breakout Godland , a sprawling exploration of Danish colonialism and Christianity in 19th-century Iceland, which premiered to international acclaim in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival. His decision to follow such an ambitious work with something as intimate, restrained, and wistful as The Love That Remains may come as a surprise, but only at first glance. Following the lives of Anna (Saga Garðarsdóttir) and Magnús (Sverrir Gudnason), a recently separated couple co-parenting their three children while navigating life beyond marriage, The Love That Remains is an epic in its own right—a deeply poetic homage to lingering feelings, the many shapes affection can take, and the role that art and dreams play in our everyday lives.

I caught up with Pálmason at Les Films de Cannes à Bucarest, a yearly retrospective of the highlights of Cannes founded by Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, which last year presented a small focus on Pálmason’s films. We discussed his cinematic signatures and open-ended working process, and the influence of canonical painters such as Claude Monet and Eugène Delacroix on his artistic techniques and worldview.

It’s surprising to see you go from a film like Godland to something that’s so much more intimate. There were hints that you were working on a film like this in your 2022 short, Nest, which follows three siblings—played by your own kids, who also appear in The Love That Remains —building a tree house over the course of a year.

Nest prompted me to begin taking The Love That Remains seriously as my next project. Because I spent two years filming my kids and this tree house, I spent much time inside a small shed, reading books or waiting for animals to come into the frame. And while I sat there, I started thinking: what are the parents of these children doing? So, I started writing a small narrative for them. However, the first thing that we shot for The Love That Remains was in 2017—the image of the roof that opens the movie. That was before Godland .

When we moved our family from Denmark to the countryside of Iceland, we bought our own film camera and accessories. I just keep the camera in the car every day and film whatever I want. This is how I construct and build my films—using the material I’ve already shot instead of writing the whole thing. I’m always shooting and then reacting, and that material is dictating what direction I’m going in.

There’s a playful critique of masculinity in The Love That Remains , following similar threads that are explored in Godland but in a very different way. For example, there is this beautiful scene when Magnús looks up Anna’s skirt where you play with the idea of the male gaze. In most films, this scene would come off as sleazy, but you transform it into such a tender and loving moment.

Being a male, I’m fascinated by these things—these basic, primitive needs and wants. I remember, early on, when we did the under-the-dress scene, someone on the team said it might be read negatively. It depends on how you do it. If it’s done with the naïve joy of beauty, then it will be expressed that way.

Your films have a very distinctive signature: the time-lapse sequences that you’ve used in the opening shots of A White, White Day (2019), in the closing sequence of Godland , and even as the structure of the entire film in Nest . In The Love That Remains, these scenes are spread throughout the film and feel somehow more self-aware and deconstructed.

I’m really interested in the seasons and the temperament of the weather: the beauty and the brutality of it, these contrasts of cold and warm, stillness and storm. I use them almost like a palette for painting, to balance the film. If there is a difficult period in a film—for example, with The Love That Remains , when it starts to become violent or dangerous, or when the relationship is sort of going sour—I can use images that lift those feelings. I use them as emotional colors in the film.

When you’re watching a film and you can feel time passing, for me, the film becomes more real. It’s like seeing something grow. It’s very emotional. I am still exploring it. I think that the next film will be the ultimate, like it will be indulged in time and space.

Those scenes remind me of the work of Monet, particularly his explorations in his garden.

It connects a lot to Monet. I remember being very inspired by the paintings and diaries of Delacroix and Paul Klee, and by much of the writing of Per Kirkeby, a Danish painter. And there’s one Spaniard from Catalonia, [Antoni] Tàpies, who wrote two memoirs. When I read these books and then saw their paintings, I responded powerfully to the very mundane things they depicted— like when they were just painting their kids taking a bath, the food they were going to eat over the weekend, or a bottle of wine. I felt emotionally stimulated by them. I felt it was beautiful, that it had to do with the ups and downs of life.

When I read their diaries, they were very normal, down-to-earth, too. “Okay, how much money do I have left to buy food? How much money do I have to buy paint? What colors am I going to buy? How is the weather outside? Is it cold? How is my health? How do I feel?” I connect with these kinds of things because it shows that, as human beings, we don’t change that much. We are the same, whether in the time of Delacroix or today.

How much were your children involved in creating their own scenes? The film borrows a lot of the kids’ humor, and it’s very authentic, very faithful to the feeling of being a child.

If something is very free, then you don’t know if it’s improvised or constructed. I’m a big fan of John Cassavetes. He had this way of making films that gave [them] a weird sense of reality. He had a long process of writing, rehearsing, and testing the scripts. That is how he constructed this spontaneity, so that the film feels fresh, authentic.

I think a lot about that and try to make my films feel authentic, especially because the camera is not handheld. Sometimes there’s some panning, but there’s no dolly, there’s nothing. It’s extremely simple and down-to-earth. We worked a lot to make the dialogue feel fluid. For example, with the kids, I would write a scene for them. Then I would give the scene to my daughter, my oldest. She worked it out with the boys. They tested it out. Later, when I was making dinner, they came and performed it. Then I maybe commented on it, maybe rewrote it a little bit, or they came with ideas, and then suddenly it worked better.

But the script, the final shooting draft for the principal photography, was extremely detailed. Every interruption, every comma, everything is there. And they are really good at nailing it, really good at having the same reactions again and again, even if we’re shooting for the third, fourth, or 20th time. There are also moments where I’m trying to capture someone blushing or reacting to something, and they might not know I’m filming them. I do that because I know that there are some things in cinema that you can’t fake, or it’s just boring to fake them.

Have your kids seen the film? How do they feel about it?

They saw it at Cannes and really liked it. That was actually one of the most beautiful things about the premiere—hearing them laugh out loud while we were watching it.

Obviously, I’m very proud of what they did in the film. But I’m also happy that it doesn’t feel confusing to them. Because they’re not interested in being actors, filmmakers, or artists. I think that attitude is very nice on screen. They don’t give a shit. They’re doing it for me. And for fun, being part of the group. And to get paid.

What are you working on next?

Right now, we’re working on a period film. It’s about the genesis of my hometown, Höfn, where I live now. It’s based on the life of a merchant named Ottó Tuliníus who lived on the other side of the mountain that the town is on. It’s the story of him and his family deconstructing their house and turning it into a raft, putting all of their stuff on it, and traveling around the mountain, by sea, to find a new place to rebuild the house. I’ve been prepping and shooting it for a year, little by little, and we’ll be filming for two more years. In a sense, it’s also like Nest , but taken to the extremes: it’s the most extreme, strangest film I’ve ever made.
excerpt_original: Family rooms: the Icelandic auteur discusses his latest intimate epic, which follows a separated couple co-parenting their children while navigating life beyond marriage

title_original: «L’arte italiana non era valutata quanto meritava». Intervista a Mariolina Bassetti per i 25 anni di Thinking Italian

Thinking Italian , il format di Christie’s dedicato all’arte italiana del XX e XXI secolo, appartiene a pieno alla seconda categoria. Non solo una presenza strutturale sulla scena internazionale – con una doppia cadenza annuale, in primavera e in autunno – ma anche un osservatorio privilegiato sulle gerarchie di valore, sulla ridefinizione dei canoni, sulla selezione consacrazione riscoperta dei suoi protagonisti. Ben oltre i confini nazionali. Il 22 ottobre, in concomitanza con Art Basel Paris, Thinking Italian torna in Avenue Matignon con un’edizione speciale che celebra i suoi primi 25 anni: 25 opere e una selezione di altissimo profilo, tra capolavori di Pistoletto, Boetti, Fontana.
